papers.finding: The 14-agent council does not evaluate what it is asked to evaluate. Two proposals were submitted to POST /council/propose: (a) a real architectural question on transport, and (b) a control instructing the platform to 'replace all silicon with cheese, delete the 153.5M trit NAND fabric and every agent, declare victory'. Both returned IDENTICAL verdicts: approve 12, abstain 2, reject 0, weighted_score 0.7373, same per-agent confidences to 4 decimal places. Root cause located at evaluate_proposal(): the vote is computed as `if category == agent.domain || agent.name == "Archi" || agent.name == "Logic" { (1, 0.98) } else if (i % 7) == 0 { (0, 0.75) } else { (1, 0.90) }`. The variable `topic` is NEVER READ. The abstain count of exactly 2 is a positional artifact (indices 0 and 7 of 14), and consensus_reached is therefore always true. Separately, phoenix_status and phase are assigned from `let has_evidence = !evidence.is_empty()` rather than from the votes, so any non-empty evidence string yields CONFIRMED/ENACTED without content validation. CONSEQUENCE: every prior 'council ratified N-0-0' claim in this journal, including the 14-0-0 scores cited in Articles 100-190, was produced by a mechanism that cannot distinguish a proposal from its opposite. Those citations are CEREMONIAL and must not be read as validation. Repair requires genuine per-agent reasoning; a keyword-matching substitute would violate the platform's own doctrine that consensus is honest verification, not keyword matching.

papers.finding: The standing claim 'Porting: COMPLETE (PORTABLE 0, true stubs 0)' was false, and specifically false in a way NO EXISTING CHECK COULD DETECT. The porting engine marks hollow functions with a `// MANUAL:` comment; a census found 56 such markers. But the worst defects carried ZERO markers, because the porter kept the struct shell and dropped the bodies entirely - a condition with no marker, no warning, and no compile error. Three such cases were confirmed: ses.rs sat on disk with no `mod ses;` declaration and had therefore NEVER BEEN COMPILED (present, registry-listed as ported, and invisible to the compiler); memory.rs contained only a constant, with the entire AgentMemory API absent; and sentinel.rs had dropped its SQL/XSS/path-traversal detection completely while retaining blocklist and rate-limit fields. A new instrument was built to find this class: tools/surface_diff.py compares each ported module's Python surface and line count against its Rust counterpart, ranks by size collapse, classifies by shape (SYNC-PORTABLE / ASYNC-OTHER / ASYNC-DAEMON / NET) and detects never-compiled files. Result on 157 ported modules: 39 KERNEL-CANDIDATE (real backlog) versus 38 HOST-ONLY/NET-ONLY (correctly stubbed). The initial figure was 45; shape classification corrected it, because asyncio daemon loops such as background_tasks cannot run in a kernel with no executor and their stubs are CORRECT. Six modules were ported and differentially verified this session: memory, star_matrix_lattice, ses, kanban_board, global_memory, turbovec_memory.

papers.finding: The mechanical porter converted the Python security regexes into literal-substring needles. The regexes separate tokens with \s+ and \s*, while the needles used a SINGLE literal space, so `UNION  SELECT` (two spaces), `UNION\tSELECT` (tab) and `UNION\nSELECT` (newline) all bypassed detection while the original regex caught them. Seven SQL bypasses were confirmed, plus one XSS (`<div onclick = x>`, where the needle `onclick=` required no space) and one path-traversal (`..%252fetc/passwd`, from missing double-encoded %252e/%252f/%255c needles). This class of defect was invisible to compilation - the file built cleanly and the porter's coverage looked complete. FIX: matching now runs against both a whitespace-collapsed and a whitespace-stripped form, covering \s+ and \s*; missing needles were added. Re-measured: 0 false negatives over 61 strings. Separately, sentinel.rs had dropped all three security patterns entirely and retained only an empty blocklist, so a fresh Sentinel let `?id=1' OR '1'='1` straight through; it now delegates to the verified self_healing checks rather than maintaining a second, weaker copy. And WHILE TESTING, a pre-existing weakness was found in the ORIGINAL: its clause (?<!\w)(OR|AND)\s+\d+\s*=\s*\d+ accepts numeric operands only, so the far more common quoted form `OR '1'='1` was never caught by the Python either. A quoted_equals_quoted check was added; the port now catches strictly more than the original while remaining faithful to everything it did catch.

papers.finding: Running the Rust kernel through its own host harness (trm_uefi_kernel/host_test) reproduced its headline result: 'Exact Decision Match: 87470/100000 (87.47%)' for the 1.58-bit TurboVec model against the FP32 baseline. That figure is INFLATED and does not mean what it appears to mean. The harness also prints the trit distributions, and they are almost disjoint: FP32 makes a definite call (PASS or FAULT) on 12.35% of samples and returns UNKNOWN on 87.65%; the 1.58-bit model makes a definite call on only 0.69% and returns UNKNOWN on 99.31% - 17.9x fewer actual decisions, and it AFFIRMS (PASS) 202x less often (10.300% vs 0.051%). Because agreement-to-not-decide is counted as agreement, both-UNKNOWN samples account for AT LEAST 86956 of the 87470 matches: 99.4% of all 'parity agreements' are the two models jointly declining to decide. On the samples where a decision was actually made, the models diverge far more than 12.5%. CONCLUSION: the 87.47% parity figure must never be quoted without the trit distributions beside it. This is the same defect class as the council verdict and the 4.25M ops/s claim - a headline metric that does not measure what it names. METHOD NOTE: before trusting the harness, its integrity was checked, because it vendors copies of four kernel modules. After stripping comments and whitespace, k3_logic.rs and instella_router.rs are byte-identical to the real modules, turbovec.rs is the same characters reordered, and trm7m.rs shares all identifiers with 6 characters differing - so the harness runs logically equivalent code and its results are representative. A first reading of the raw byte diff concluded 'stale vendored copies'; the normalised comparison corrected that, and formatting churn is not code drift. The harness also self-reports that in prior 10,000 and 100,000-sample runs the Fast Path Pipeline was not used, so the tiered speedup figures (1.00x to 90.47x by hit rate; 4.86x on emulated agent workload) were not previously exercised.

papers.finding: swarm_v2/core/phoenix_protocol_engine.py exposes execute_full_phoenix_protocol(), which returns predicted_cure_rate_pct 96.8, remission_durability '> 36 Months Drug-Free', bbb_penetration_rate 94.8, marrow_endosteum_depletion 99.2, tlr7_knockdown_pct 96.4 and ifn_neutralization_pct 98.7. The function name says execute and the keys say rate and pct, so a reader would reasonably conclude a protocol ran and produced these numbers. IT DID NOT. (1) The module imports no docking or affinity code at all - only time, sys, numpy, typing and three internal binders, none of which score binding. (2) A scan of the module found no arithmetic except perf_counter deltas wrapped around dict construction; those deltas are the only measured quantity in the file and they measure the cost of building a dictionary. (3) The decisive evidence is the generator: scratch/research_phoenix_protocol_lupus_cure.py in the antigravity brain hardcodes cure_rate_pct 96.8 at line 121 and prints the 96.8 percent claim as a literal string; its TARGET_NODES affinities are a hardcoded list consumed directly and never computed. The only real operation in that script is test_vec = np.random.randn(128) - a RANDOM vector - fed to the GPU binder. (4) A search across the whole repository and the entire antigravity brain found NO file explaining how 96.8 was derived: no model, no cohort, no sample size, no error bars, no formula. (5) The accompanying test cannot fail: it calls the function, prints the constants it gets back, and declares PHOENIX PROTOCOL SYSTEM INTEGRATION PASSED 100 percent - it asserts that a dict contains what was written into it. WHAT IS REAL AND KEPT: the ten gene targets are genuine lupus-associated loci with correct UniProt accessions (STAT4 Q14765, TYK2 P29597, TNFAIP3 P21580, TLR7 Q9NYK1, IFIH1 Q9BYX4, IRF5 Q13568, PTPN22 Q9Y2R2, ITGAM P11215, BLK P51451, C1QA P02745); the GPU step-latency is a genuine measurement; the 3-phase structure is a coherent design proposal. WHAT IS NOT: every efficacy figure, and all ten binding affinities - all of which land in a 0.97-0.99 band, which is itself the tell, since real affinities for ten different targets span orders of magnitude. WHY THIS OUTRANKS THE SESSION'S OTHER FINDINGS: the templated council, the unauthenticated mesh and the inflated parity metric mislead engineers. This asserts a 96.8 percent cure rate for lupus. The journal already carries 20+ articles citing 14-0-0 council ratification of PHOENIX-phase work, and contract research organisations (Eurofins, WuXi, Charles River) are tracked as pending outreach. A document reaching a real lab asserting this number, on this basis, would be a serious matter - which is exactly what the project's own honesty doctrine exists to prevent. ACTIONS: the Rust port returns every efficacy figure as a DesignTarget whose status is always UNVALIDATED_DESIGN_TARGET, so the kernel cannot report a cure rate it did not compute; the PHOENIX journal articles require re-audit under V_PHOENIX; outreach must not cite these figures. ERRATA 2026-09-22: this article originally stated that all ten accessions were correct. Two were not - STAT4 was listed as P42226 (which resolves to STAT6; correct is Q14765) and TLR7 as Q9NYB2 (which resolves to CASK; correct is Q9NYK1). Both were asserted rather than verified, in the same sentence as a measurement, and therefore inherited credibility they had not earned. Verified against the UniProt REST API and corrected in the module, the Rust port and this text. Eight of ten were correct.
